findings.matters: A finance director can compare the council's projected Core Spending Power growth with the national settlement assumptions, and see where the paper warns those assumptions may not match local income.

findings.headline: Assets previously revalued as Property, Plant and Equipment were transferred to investment property, with a fair value of £61.75m and £1.184m of rental income in the year.
findings.detail: After a review of the asset portfolio, the council reclassified assets as investment property at fair value, with gains or losses recognised in financing and investment income. The fair value is based on market evidence and is categorised at Level 2.
findings.matters: A reclassification of this size moves value between the balance sheet categories a lender or finance director reads, so it affects how the asset base is presented.

findings.matters: A finance director comparing capital delivery can use the scale of spend and the mix of general fund schemes as a benchmark.

findings.matters: The gap between carrying value and fair value shows how much the council's fixed-rate debt is worth below market, which affects refinancing and early-repayment decisions across the sector.

findings.paper_title: 3.1 - 26 LBTH Interim VFM report September 2026
findings.headline: Revised Minimum Revenue Provision policy defers capital financing costs to future years, reducing budget flexibility from 2050 onwards.
findings.detail: The Council changed its MRP policy in 2024/25 to charge capital financing costs disproportionately toward later years of asset life. This delivered a £7.7 million short-term benefit to the General Fund in 2025/26 (charged £3.96 million against £11.7 million budget), but Ernst & Young concluded this does not represent a prudent approach. The Council acknowledged that by 2059/60, the existing budget will no longer be sufficient. Without this policy change, the council would face additional pressures of up to £27 million across the medium-term financial plan to 2028/29.
findings.matters: Deferring capital costs is a short-term fix that disguises underlying deficits rather than addressing them; it increases future borrowing requirements and reduces flexibility to respond to future shocks.
findings.figures: 2025/26 MRP charge £3.96 million against budget of £11.7 million (£7.7 million saving); £27 million additional pressure across MTFS 2026-29 without policy change; existing budget insufficient by 2059/60
findings.quote: We have concluded that the application of the Council's revised MRP policy did not represent a prudent approach, resulting in MRP charges being profiled disproportionately towards the later years of an asset's economic life.

findings.matters: A 33% reserves position provides minimal financial buffer against shocks or service pressures; severely constrains the council's flexibility and ability to repay borrowing if service income falls.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report - 2025-26
findings.headline: Interest rate and economic outlook significantly uncertain due to geopolitical events affecting treasury assumptions
findings.detail: The financial year experienced significant volatility from US tariff announcements in April 2025 and the Iran war in late February 2026. The latter caused sharp rises in gilt yields and oil prices. The council's treasury adviser (Arlingclose) has revised interest rate forecasts with explicit acknowledgement that forecasts may change frequently as the situation evolves. The council's borrowing cost assumptions were developed under previous rate forecasts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's treasury strategy and financing cost assumptions are sensitive to interest rate movements. Significant rate changes would materially affect the viability of the planned borrowing programme and debt serviceability.

findings.headline: Investment income outperformance of £1.7m masks temporary benefit from inverted yield curve
findings.detail: The council earned £6.58m in investment income against a budget of £4.88m—an outperformance of £1.708m or 35%. This was achieved because short-term interest rates exceeded long-term rates during the year, allowing the council to earn attractive returns on cash holdings and short-term instruments. Externally managed strategic pooled funds contributed £3.06m in total return.
findings.matters: The outperformance has materially improved the council's 2025/26 position and helped offset costs. However, this benefit is contingent on the inverted yield curve and will likely diminish if Bank Rate falls as historically expected, creating a headwind for future financing capacity.
findings.figures: Investment income £6.58m actual vs £4.88m budget (outperformance £1.708m); total return on investments 5.87%; strategic pooled fund return £3.06m
findings.quote: The Council has benefitted from higher short-term interest rates for treasury investments, which have seen an overachievement in interest income received. A total of £6.58m was earned against a £4.88m budget. This has been possible as average short-term rates were above average long-term rates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026-27 Period 2 Savings Portfolio Tracker
findings.headline: £11.9m of £69.8m savings target (17%) marked subject to delivery risk or unlikely to deliver in 2026/27
findings.detail: Out of the full-year savings target, £7.8m is marked 'at risk' and £4.1m 'unlikely', representing 17% of the plan. This leaves a material funding gap if these savings do not materialise.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can actually balance its budget as planned, or whether it faces a shortfall that could require further cuts or reserves draw.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Council has introduced enhanced financial governance (Spending Review Panels, Expenditure Control Panels, Financial Sustainability Forum) signaling recognition of severity
findings.detail: In response to the scale of financial pressures, the council created a Financial Sustainability Forum (chaired by the Mayor), Spending Review Panels, and Expenditure Control Panels to scrutinize spending and savings delivery. Three dedicated boards were established for Temporary Accommodation, Adult Social Care, and SEND. These governance layers suggest the council recognizes it is losing control of spending.
findings.matters: While governance improvements are positive, the need to create them suggests the council previously lacked adequate financial controls and is now in catch-up mode. The fact that controls are needed at this level indicates the severity of the problem.
findings.figures: Financial Sustainability Forum established; Spending Review Panels (chaired by Mayor); Expenditure Control Panels (£10k+ threshold for corporate review); three dedicated pressure boards
findings.quote: The Council has introduced several key financial governance arrangements during the year, that will strengthen control and drive down these costs. This includes Expenditure Control Panels to review all Council spending proposals, People Resourcing Board to review all staffing requests and Spending Review Panels to scrutinise Directorate finances.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Income volatility in Planning & Building Control (£2.0m underspend) and Leisure (£2.0m shortfall) shows reliance on uncertain revenue streams
findings.detail: Planning & Building Control achieved a £2.0m underspend, but this masks high volatility: planning fee income fluctuates with development pipeline, with schemes 'delayed, stalled, mothballed or do not materialise'. Leisure services underspent by £2.0m due to income shortfall against budget. These are core income sources but vulnerable to economic cycles.
findings.matters: The council's budget contains significant reliance on income streams (planning, leisure, commercial rents) that are neither controllable nor countercyclical, increasing financial fragility in a downturn.
findings.figures: Planning & Building Control: £2.0m underspend but vulnerable to development pipeline; Leisure services: £2.0m income shortfall; 87% income-funded for P&BC
findings.quote: Planning and Building Control is primarily income funded and is reliant on the development pipeline for the majority of its funding. The development industry and property markets remain very challenging and consequently puts pressure on this pipeline if projects, as is happening, are delayed, stalled, mothballed or do not materialise.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage: GF capital only 86.9% spent and HRA capital only 70.2% spent, suggesting delivery weakness
findings.detail: General Fund capital outturn was £51.5m of £59.3m revised budget (86.9% delivery), with £7.8m variance. HRA capital was £130.1m of £185.3m revised budget (70.2% delivery), with £55.2m variance. This pattern of slippage across both programmes suggests systemic delays in project delivery and capital planning.
findings.matters: Repeated capital under-spending indicates the council's capital programme is not realistic or projects face systemic delivery challenges. This affects both asset renewal and service capacity.
findings.figures: GF capital: £51.5m spent of £59.3m budget (86.9%, £7.8m variance); HRA capital: £130.1m of £185.3m (70.2%, £55.2m variance); HRA New Build: £26.7m of £46.4m (57.6%, £19.7m re-profile)
findings.quote: The General Fund capital provisional outturn for the year is £51.5m, which represents 86.9% of the revised 2025/26 capital budget of £59.3m, resulting in a net variance of (£7.8m) at year-end.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Savings target only 91% achieved, with £2.7m (9%) requiring re-phasing into future years
findings.detail: Of £30.2m in-year savings targets, only £27.5m (91%) was delivered. £2.7m of savings failed to materialize and require re-profiling. This means the council is not meeting its own efficiency targets and is running behind on cost reduction, necessitating reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver its own planned savings is one that is not in control of its cost base and will struggle to meet medium-term financial targets.
findings.figures: £30.2m savings target; £27.5m achieved (91%); £2.7m rephased (9%)
findings.quote: Of the £30.2m in-year savings target, £27.5m (91%) was achieved, while £2.7m (9%) has not been achieved in-year and requires re-profiling.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Children's Social Care Supporting Families overspend of £13.7m from increased demand, complexity, and placement costs
findings.detail: Supporting Families overspent by £13.7m, representing a £9.5m adverse movement from Q3 forecast alone. Key drivers include 13 additional children in residential care requiring high-cost placements, pressures in supported accommodation for care leavers and unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, and agency staffing costs for specialist roles.
findings.matters: This service is experiencing volatile demand spikes (£9.5m deterioration in one quarter) and the council cannot forecast or control placement market costs. This is a signature of structural under-budgeting.
findings.figures: £13.7m overspend; £9.5m adverse movement from Q3 alone; 13 additional residential placements in Q4 alone
findings.quote: The most significant movement relates to residential care, where expenditure increased by £2.0m following an additional 13 children requiring residential placements during the final quarter.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserves falling toward minimum threshold, reduced from £34.1m to £21.5m in one year
findings.detail: HRA reserves fell by £12.6m net in-year to £21.5m, only £11.5m above the £10m minimum reserve threshold. The council is using reserves to fund capital works (planned RCCO of £24m budgeted vs £12.1m actual) and absorb operational pressures including building safety compliance costs and temporary accommodation pressures.
findings.matters: The HRA is approaching its minimum reserve threshold with little headroom. Building safety and legislative compliance costs are structural and ongoing, leaving little flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA reserves: opened £34.1m, closed £21.5m (£12.6m drawdown); minimum threshold £10m; actual RCCO £12.1m vs £24m budgeted
findings.quote: After applying this net reserve drawdown, the reserve balance held has reduced from £34.1m to £21.5m, against an approved minimum balance of £10m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Risk reserve depleted to £4.9m at year-end after £18.6m drawdown, down from £21.6m
findings.detail: The council created a risk reserve of £21.6m to absorb demand-driven pressures. This has been drawn down by the full year-end overspend (£18.6m), leaving just £4.9m in contingency. Total General Fund and earmarked reserves stand at £111.7m, but after the DSG liability (£3.5m) and ongoing overspends, reserves are eroding at pace.
findings.matters: The council has little capacity to absorb further adverse movements. A single bad year in housing or social care, or external shock, will exhaust reserves.
findings.figures: Risk reserve: opened £1.9m, topped up to £21.6m, closed at £4.9m (£18.6m drawdown); total GF and earmarked reserves £111.7m
findings.quote: The provisional outturn General Fund and earmarked reserves position is summarised in Table 3 below. The provisional outturn net overspend of £18.6m at year-end has been funded from the risk reserve. This would leave the Council with a risk reserve of £4.9m at year-end.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit of £35.2m, with £3.5m residual liability falling to reserves when statutory override ends in 2027/28
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £15.1m in 2025/26, bringing the cumulative deficit to £35.2m. Government will write off 90% subject to a SEND reform plan, but Tower Hamlets' 10% residual of £3.5m must be funded from reserves when the statutory override expires in 2027/28. The policy on residuals and new accruals after that date remains unclear.
findings.matters: A £3.5m liability is certain to fall on reserves in less than 18 months, further eroding the council's financial buffer. This is a known, quantified future drain on cash.
findings.figures: £15.1m in-year overspend; £35.2m cumulative deficit; £3.5m residual (10%) to be funded from reserves; statutory override ends 2027/28
findings.quote: Government proposes to write off 90% of DSG High Needs deficits accrued to 31 March 2026 (subject to Autumn 2026 DfE plan approval). Tower Hamlets' residual 10% is £3.5m and may fall to reserves when the statutory override ends in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £22.2m driven by increased complexity and volumes that exceed demographic forecasts
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £22.2m, with Homecare at £9.9m and Supported Living at £7.0m of the overspend. The council reports a 12% increase in service users and that inflationary pressures exceeded budget by £5.1m on top of an £8.9m demand pressure beyond demographic forecasts. The strategic shift to independent living is 'materially more expensive in the short to medium term'.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly stated its demographic forecasts were understated and market costs are outpacing assumptions. This suggests budget-setting is not responsive to real demand and will remain under pressure.
findings.figures: £22.2m overspend; 12% increase in Homecare/Supported Living service users; £5.1m inflationary pressure vs £3.2m forecast; £8.9m demographic growth beyond POPPI/PANSI models
findings.quote: Market inflation was initially forecast at £3.2m within the MTFS; however, the outturn included £5.1m following a review of provider fee uplifts. This increase is largely driven by national insurance changes, workforce cost pressures, and higher-than-anticipated fee uplifts required to maintain provider sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: Housing and Homelessness overspend of £25.6m with 3,145 households in temporary accommodation against a budget for 2,409
findings.detail: Housing Options and Homelessness overspent by £25.6m, with actual temporary accommodation numbers at 3,145 against budgeted 2,409. The overspend reflects higher accommodation costs (rents now above 2011 LHA levels), use of expensive nightly-paid accommodation, and a £4.3m Housing Benefit subsidy loss. The service is investing £3.6m in landlord incentive payments to secure 500 PRS units as a mitigation.
findings.matters: This represents structural demand that has not been budgeted adequately and is driving recurring large overspends. The reliance on expensive emergency accommodation and volatile private rental market means this pressure is difficult to control.
findings.figures: £25.6m overspend; 3,145 households in TA vs 2,409 budgeted; £20.9m overspend on accommodation budgets; £4.3m Housing Benefit subsidy loss forecast
findings.quote: The budget is based on 2,409 households in TA, but the actual number stands at 3,145. This, combined with limited move-on options and rising accommodation costs, continues to place pressure on accommodation budgets.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 - Provisional Outturn
findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £18.6m for second consecutive year, following £16.5m overspend in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council spent £18.6m more than budget after applying £26m in funding substitutions and £18m in reserve drawdowns. This follows a £16.5m overspend in the prior year. The council is drawing down reserves to cover structural budget gaps rather than managing within budget.
findings.matters: Repeated large overspends of this scale signal that the council's budget is not based on realistic spending assumptions and reserves are being used to paper over operational deficits rather than for contingency. This is unsustainable.
findings.figures: £18.6m overspend 2025/26 (£16.5m in 2024/25), after £26.0m funding substitutions and £18.0m reserve drawdowns
findings.quote: The provisional outturn position is: £19.4m net General Fund (GF) overspend (£0.8m adverse movement from Q3, which was an £18.6m overspend). The adverse movement from Q3 has been offset by a £0.8m favourable movement within the Council's core funding.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: HRA facing unprecedented cost pressures from building safety, Awaab's Law, and void property costs, with minimal operational headroom
findings.detail: HRA forecasts £1.2m overspend from building safety works (£1.4m overspend including £1.1m waking watch on Cranbrook estate), void property costs (£0.9m non-dwelling repairs and security), and feasibility costs for Mayors Accelerated Housing Programme (£1.5m). Reserve position already tight, limiting ability to manage compliance costs.
findings.matters: Building safety and Awaab's Law are regulatory obligations; the council cannot avoid these costs. With minimal HRA reserves, any escalation in compliance costs will require General Fund support.
findings.figures: £1.2m HRA overspend; £1.4m building safety overspend; £1.1m waking watch Cranbrook; £0.9m void non-dwelling costs; £1.5m housing programme feasibility

Building Safety works are forecast to overspend by £1.4m due to the wide-ranging requirements of safety works to be undertaken to ensure the stock is compliant from a building and fire safety perspective.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL

findings.detail: 2026/27 Council Tax cash collection stands at £37.6m (17% collection rate) against a profiled target of 18.61%. Full-year 2025/26 collection was 92.08%, below London average of 94.5%. The council is implementing targeted early intervention and collection initiatives but has not closed the benchmark gap. Meanwhile, Local Council Tax Reduction Scheme costs rising (£38.1m, +£1.6m on prior year) due to continued demand, demonstrating sustained pressure on low-income residents.
findings.matters: Council Tax undercollection reduces certainty of revenue. Collection below London peers is a red flag for underlying economic distress in the borough and/or collection effectiveness issues.
findings.figures: 17% collection rate (1.61% below target); 2025/26 92.08% (below London 94.5%); LCTRS cost £38.1m (+£1.6m); 27,836 households on LCTRS

Council Tax collection improved to 92.08% in 2025/26... although it continues to sit below the London averages for 94.5%.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Risk Reserve declining to £16m headroom, with Housing Revenue Account reserves at £10.4m against £10m minimum floor, leaving minimal buffer for adverse variances
findings.detail: General Fund Risk Reserve forecast to close at £16m (including £4.9m brought forward), down from £20m budgeted contribution being diverted to offset overspend. HRA reserves forecast to £10.4m after £11.1m drawdown to cover £1.2m operational overspend, leaving only £0.4m headroom against the £10m minimum. Any further adverse variances force additional drawdowns.
findings.matters: Declining reserves limit the council's ability to manage in-year volatility or respond to unexpected pressures; minimal HRA headroom is a particular concern given building safety and Awaab's Law compliance costs.

However, this will need to increase to £11.1m due to a forecast in-year overspend of £1.2m... This reduces reserve balances to £10.4m, against a minimum level of £10m. This gives little headroom for further overspends.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL

findings.detail: Of planned 2026/27 savings, £29.2m achieved, £28.7m on track, £7.8m at risk, £4.1m unlikely (11% + 6% at risk or lost). Housing Options carries £4.8m in new savings proposals (moving households from TA) that are explicitly flagged as having delivery risk; if not delivered, overspend rises from £6.6m to £11.4m.
findings.matters: Savings delivery is already tracking behind plan; losses here would push the overall General Fund position into further deficit.

findings.quote: £7.8m (11%) of savings are currently at risk, but corrective actions are being deployed to put them back on track. £4.1m (6%) of savings is forecasted as unlikely to be delivered.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £14.2m driven by placement demand exceeding funding, with pessimistic scenario worsening to £17m
findings.detail: Supporting Families division forecasts £14.7m overspend with 32 children in high-cost residential placements and significant reliance on independent fostering agencies due to market capacity constraints and inflation. Service actively deploying £4m in mitigations but risks exist to delivery. Pessimistic scenario (continued growth in children entering care plus market inflation) escalates position to £17m.
findings.matters: Like ASC, children's placement demand and costs are structural, inflation-driven, and constrained by limited market supply; they are hard to control through management action alone.
findings.figures: £14.2m net forecast overspend; 32 children in residential care; £12.2m residential care pressure; £2.3m fostering; £4m mitigations identified; £17m worst-case scenario
findings.quote: The Supporting Families Division is forecasting a £14.7m overspend. The principal pressures comprise £12.2m within Residential Care, where the service is currently supporting 32 children in high-cost residential placements with complex needs. A further £2.3m pressure relates to fostering, reflecting continued reliance on independent fostering agencies due to limited placement availability and strong market demand, which has driven significant fee inflation.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £83m by 2028, with cumulative High Needs block deficit growing from £35.2m opening balance to £59.1m by year-end
findings.detail: The DSG account shows a £21.7m in-year overspend in 2026/27, with the High Needs block (specialist SEND placements) accounting for £23.9m of that. Cumulative deficit forecast to reach £83m by end of 2028/29. The council's SEND Reform Plan submission to DfE could unlock a grant to write off 90% of the £35.2m brought-forward deficit, but the 10% unfunded element (£3.5m) remains the council's liability. Government has indicated future support will be conditional on successful delivery of reform plans.
findings.matters: The DSG override protecting councils from General Fund impact ends April 2028; if only 90% write-off is granted, the council faces a £8.3m one-off cost in 2028/29 on top of structural pressures.
findings.figures: £21.7m 2026/27 overspend; £56.9m closing cumulative deficit; £83m forecast 2028/29; £35.2m High Needs brought-forward; £3.5m unfunded (10%); potential £8.3m cost if 10% must be funded
findings.quote: If 10% of the deficits for 2026/27 and 2027/28 are also required to be funded by the Council, then £8.3m (10% of £83m) will be required to be included in the budget as a one-off cost in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £10.4m driven by demographic pressures and care provider inflation that show no sign of abating
findings.detail: HASC directorate forecast £10.4m net overspend due to 13% increase in homecare clients, sustained growth in supported living costs (cost of shift away from residential to independent living is higher in short term), and demographic pressures of £3.5m exceeding MTFS assumptions. The council faces an unfunded cumulative gap of £2.8m from prior years. Pessimistic scenario (1% higher growth) deteriorates position by £3.9m to £14.3m.
findings.matters: ASC demand is growing faster than funding; the council cannot solve this through short-term actions and it will persist across future financial years.
findings.figures: £10.4m net overspend; 13% increase in homecare clients; £3.5m demographic pressure; £2.8m unfunded cumulative gap; £1.5m savings slippage
findings.quote: The costs of Adult Social Care accounts for £7.8m of the overspend... Supported Living costs across Learning Disability and Mental Health services are also increasing significantly. While the strategic shift away from residential care towards more independent living arrangements is aligned with national policy and delivers improved outcomes for individuals, it is materially more expensive in the short to medium term.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs forecast £6.6m overspend with 3,164 households; homelessness demand up 9%; private rental market creates £3.4m Housing Benefit subsidy loss
findings.detail: Housing Options forecasts a £6.6m overspend driven by 3,164 households in temporary accommodation (TA), with homelessness demand up 9% and the Renters Rights Act triggering a surge in section 21 evictions. The council expects TA eviction cases to peak in Q2-Q3. Market rents now significantly exceed Housing Benefit subsidy levels, creating a £3.4m subsidy loss. New £4.8m savings proposals assume moving households out of TA, but carry delivery risk.
findings.matters: TA is one of the largest uncontrollable budget lines for councils; a forecast peak in evictions and demand that already exceeds budget signals a structural cost problem a lender needs to model for.
findings.figures: 3,164 households in TA; 9% demand forecast increase; £6.6m overspend; £3.4m Housing Benefit subsidy loss; £4.8m in new savings (at risk)
findings.quote: We are expecting that 2026/27 will be a year of fluctuation due to the PRS markets and landlord behavior adapting to the new norm. This makes forecasting more difficult, requiring a detailed, realistic and focused appraisal... the main driver of the overspend remains the cost of nightly paid accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2026-27 Period 2 Report FINAL
findings.headline: Repeated substantial overspends being masked by reserve drawdowns rather than solved through budget action
findings.detail: Tower Hamlets forecast £19.2m overspend in 2026/27, following an £18.6m overspend in 2025/26. Rather than identifying recurrent savings, the council is drawing down £8.9m from the Risk Reserve and £6.5m of contingency to offset the deficit, leaving the underlying budget gap unsolved.
findings.matters: Lenders fund councils expecting budget stability; repeated use of one-off reserves to balance budgets signals structural problems and shrinking financial headroom.
findings.figures: £19.2m forecast overspend 2026/27; £18.6m overspend 2025/26; £8.9m Risk Reserve drawdown; £6.5m contingency used
findings.quote: The net forecast overspend at Period 2 for the year is £19.2m, including net transfer to reserves of £7.0m... Officers are instructed to identify additional in-year mitigations to minimise any further drawdown from reserves.

findings.headline: External auditor issued formal statutory recommendations—financial reporting arrangements found deficient
findings.detail: EY issued three statutory recommendations for the year ended 31 March 2024. On financial reporting, the auditor found the council lacked sufficient and appropriate audit evidence for transactions in the financial statements, and has not been timely in implementing prior audit findings.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations (escalated to the Secretary of State) indicate control environment failures that undermine the reliability of reported financial position.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued by external auditor EY
findings.quote: take action to ensure that sufficient and appropriate audit evidence is available in relation to transactions in the financial statements

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Appendix C - Capital Strategy Report Council
findings.headline: Multiple capital project cancellations and deferrals indicating delivery and affordability pressures
findings.detail: The council has cancelled or substantially delayed several major capital schemes. The Institute of Academic Excellence project (£15m) is no longer progressing as the site has been reallocated to the Mayor's Accelerated Housing Programme. The George Green/Westferry project (£551k) is under review pending a refreshed Project Initiation Document due to significantly different design costs. The Lochnagar Bridge project was abandoned after the partner borough could not acquire the necessary landing point and Levelling Up funding faced expiry.
findings.matters: Project cancellations suggest either financial discipline in reining back unaffordable commitments or execution/planning risk; delivery of the remaining £319.6m capital programme as planned is material to service continuity and financial forecasts
findings.figures: Institute of Academic Excellence budget released: £15.0m; George Green/Westferry under review: £551k; Lochnagar Bridge: project abandoned with funding redirected
findings.quote: The PDC site is now included within the Mayor's Accelerated Housing Programme as a housing project. As a result, the Institute of Academic Excellence project is no longer progressing with the full budget to be released (£15.0m).

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Appendix C - Capital Strategy Report Council
findings.headline: Liquid reserves being drawn down from £176m to £60m minimum to fund capital programme
findings.detail: Treasury investments (cash surplus held for contingency and spending needs) are forecast to decline sharply from £176m actual at 31 March 2025 to £60m by 31 March 2026 and maintained at this minimum thereafter. Near-term investments alone are dropping from £120m to £4m. This £116m drawdown represents the council using accumulated reserves to fund capital spending rather than relying entirely on new borrowing.
findings.matters: Running reserves down to a £60m minimum substantially reduces the council's financial flexibility to manage unexpected revenue shortfalls or spending pressures; increases reliance on borrowing markets for liquidity
findings.figures: Total treasury investments: £176.000m (31.3.2025) to £60.000m (31.3.2026 onwards); Near-term investments: £120.000m to £4.000m; Planned minimum: £60m cash and investments at year-end
findings.quote: This assumes that cash and investment balances are kept to a minimum level of £60m at each year-end.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Appendix C - Capital Strategy Report Council
findings.headline: Council total debt forecast to increase from £196.924m to £413.843m by 2028/29, nearly doubling over three years
findings.detail: Council borrowing is escalating sharply across both HRA and General Fund to finance the capital programme. Total debt (comprising borrowing, PFI liabilities and leases) is forecast to more than double from £196.924m in 2025/26 to £413.843m in 2028/29. General Fund financing costs are also rising from 1.2% to 3.6% of net revenue stream. The Capital Financing Requirement for the council is forecast to grow from £648.637m to £851.771m over the same period.
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating debt materially increases the council's financial leverage, debt servicing risk, and exposure to interest rate movements; constrains future borrowing capacity and fiscal flexibility
findings.quote: The Council's estimated CFR is as follows: Total CFR 629.271 648.637 671.696 723.069 851.771 (for years 2024/25 to 2028/29)

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Appendix C - Capital Strategy Report Council
findings.headline: HRA financing costs rising to 14.2% of net revenue stream by 2028/29, driven by housing acquisition and development programme
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is pursuing a major capital programme including the Mayor's Accelerated Housing Programme (£122.5m for 175 homes), acquisition of 237 homes largely completed, temporary accommodation expansion (£37.5m for 50 homes), and 17 live development schemes delivering 868 new homes. HRA financing costs are forecast to rise from £8.264m in 2025/26 to £20.375m in 2028/29, consuming 14.2% of net HRA revenue stream by 2028/29 compared to 6.4% in 2025/26.
findings.matters: By 2028/29 HRA debt servicing will consume nearly 1 in 7 pounds of HRA revenue; while HRA is ring-fenced, financial distress would cascade to the general fund and council creditworthiness
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: £8.264m (2025/26 forecast) to £20.375m (2028/29); HRA Capital Financing Requirement: £209.524m (2025/26) to £377.246m (2028/29); MAHP budget: £122.500m
findings.quote: A new addition to the HRA capital programme is the Mayor's Accelerated Housing Programme (MAHP). This programme has an allocated budget provision of £122.500m, which currently proposes 175 additional homes

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Appendix 12 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy 26-27
findings.headline: Entire £4.159m transformation funding strategy funded from unallocated capital receipts with no reserved capital projects as fallback.
findings.detail: The Council plans to apply up to £4.159m from capital receipts (care technology £659k, redundancy £3m, Power BI £500k). No capital projects are reserved as alternative uses for these receipts. If capital receipts from asset sales fall short, these transformation programmes have no revenue budget protection and must be cut.
findings.matters: Council's efficiency and transformation strategy is entirely dependent on property sale proceeds; weak asset sales would force immediate cuts to workforce support or service improvements.
findings.figures: £4.159m total 2026-27 allocation; prior year (2024-25) applied £2.1m
findings.quote: As any receipts used have not been earmarked as funding for any other proposed capital expenditure there is no impact on the Council's prudential indicators as set out in the Council's Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Appendix 12 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy 26-27
findings.headline: Care technology expansion targets 4,400 users by end of five-year programme from current 1,800, betting on preventing more expensive social care interventions.
findings.detail: Council is investing £659k in 2026-27 on care technology transformation with projected £2 benefit per £1 invested. 88% of projected savings are claimed to come from 'prevention and delay of packages of care that would otherwise have been required' in homecare and residential care. This depends on achieving adoption rates and service model shifts not yet proven at scale.
findings.matters: Social care cost pressure is material to council financial sustainability; success of this programme is uncertain and depends on residents adopting technology and accepting different care models.
findings.figures: £659k investment 2026-27; expansion from 1,800 to 4,400 users; projected £2 net benefit per £1 invested
findings.quote: For every £1 of investment it is expected there will be £2 of net benefits to the Council, from reduced, delayed or prevented needs that would have required care services to be put in place.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Appendix 12 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy 26-27
findings.headline: Early redundancy budget increased to £3m for 2026-27 (from £1.813m spent in 2024-25) with no upper limit on rolling scheme.
findings.detail: Council has committed to a rolling voluntary redundancy and early retirement programme that started in 2024-25 and continues indefinitely into future years. The £3m allocation for 2026-27 is described as 'indicative' to 'ensure the flexibility can be maximised' but the actual spend depends on 'the number of agreed departures'. This represents a significant and unpredictable one-off cost.
findings.matters: Large personnel costs funded by one-off capital receipts suggest underlying revenue budget pressures; if redundancy spend is rising annually, it indicates structural cost problems rather than transformation delivering permanent savings.
findings.quote: The scheme commenced in 2024-25 and continues on a rolling basis into future years. It is intended this provision can support the costs of all transformation related redundancy costs in the year.

findings.paper_title: 7 Appointment of interim s151
findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer role filled on interim basis after being identified as hard to recruit
findings.detail: Tower Hamlets has appointed Richard Ennis as interim Corporate Director of Resources (S151 role) for six months from 3 March 2026. The council explicitly identifies the S151 position as 'recognised as a hard to recruit role in a labour market where the necessary skills are scarce', and engaged external executive search agencies to source candidates. The appointment is framed as providing 'greater capacity and capability to progress strategic plans' while permanent recruitment takes place.
findings.matters: Difficulty recruiting the chief finance officer role—particularly on a permanent basis—may signal underlying concerns about the council's financial position or working environment that affect candidate attraction. The interim appointment creates a transition period in financial leadership that lenders would want to monitor.
findings.figures: Six month appointment from 3 March 2026
findings.quote: The Section 151 (Chief Financial Officer) is recognised as a hard to recruit role in a labour market where the necessary skills are scarce.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Children in care numbers at 2,400 with rising demand for statutory services and growing complexity of needs
findings.detail: Tower Hamlets is managing 2,400 children in care, with the budget noting that 'demand for statutory services locally is also rising, presenting an ongoing risk' and that 'the number of children with complex needs is growing, which places further strain on social care placements.' These high-cost packages are creating budget pressures, particularly given the higher property and staffing costs in London.
findings.matters: Children's social care is a high-cost, volatile demand driver. Rising complexity and placement costs create forward liability that is difficult to forecast or control.
findings.figures: 2,400 children within Tower Hamlets in care; growing complex needs; high-cost specialist provision required
findings.quote: Nationally, trends show a continuing rise in demand for Children's Social Care, creating significant spending pressures as high‑cost individual care packages increasingly impact budgets... demand for statutory services locally is also rising, presenting an ongoing risk.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Settlement is one-year only with indicative figures for 2027-29, creating planning uncertainty for councils with volatile demand patterns
findings.detail: Despite the government publishing indicative figures for 2027-29, the Final Local Government Finance Settlement is formally a one-year settlement. Tower Hamlets faces significant demand volatility in homelessness, children's and adult social care. The indicative nature of years 2-3 means any material change to government policy or funding allocation could force rapid budget resets.
findings.matters: A council reliant on year-on-year settlements with volatile demand cannot plan confidently beyond 12 months. This is particularly problematic where transformation programmes require multi-year delivery.
findings.figures: Settlement period 2026-27 to 2028-29; first year confirmed; years 2-3 indicative only
findings.quote: The settlement provides the Council with its funding allocation via Core Spending Power (CSP) from central government. It is a one-year settlement although figures for the next two years were also given as a guide.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Council is creating new reserves (Transformation Reserve £5m/year, Corporate Funding Reserve £7.6m) while relying on undelivered transformation savings
findings.detail: Alongside the £50m increase to Risk Reserve over the MTFS, the council is creating a new £5m per annum Transformation Reserve and a new £7.6m Corporate Funding Reserve. These reserve commitments total over £25m across the period while simultaneously relying on transformation programmes that are only in 'Discovery' phase to deliver £20m+ in savings.
findings.matters: Creating reserves while simultaneously relying on undelivered savings suggests the council is hedging against transformation failure, indicating awareness of delivery risk.
findings.figures: Transformation Reserve £5m per year; Corporate Funding Reserve £7.6m over MTFS; Risk Reserve increase £20m per year (£50m over MTFS); General Fund reserve minimum maintained at £25m
findings.quote: Created a Transformation Reserve of £5m a year to support delivery of major transformations. Created a Corporate Funding Reserve of £7.6m over the MTFS for funding variation risks.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care client numbers rising 10% year-on-year with estimated pressures of £23m against £22.5m growth allocation
findings.detail: Adult Social Care has 4,780 clients receiving care, up 10% from the previous year. Estimated recurring pressures are £23m but the council has only allocated £22.5m of growth funding (comprised of £10m structural, £7.5m inflationary, £5m demographic). Care provider inflation driven by London Living Wage (set to increase 6.9% next year) creates further pressure on the narrow margin.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest demand-driven budget and the council's margin against pressures is minimal. Hospital discharge changes are shifting NHS costs to the council without confirmed additional funding.
findings.figures: ASC client numbers 4,780 (10% increase from prior year); estimated recurring pressures £23.0m; growth provided £22.5m (of which £5m demographic, £7.5m inflation, £10m structural); London Living Wage increase 6.9% next year (£13.85 to £14.80/hour)
findings.quote: Reduction in NHS funding for short-term care costs following hospital discharge has shifted financial responsibility to local authorities... Demand continues to rise, driven by population growth and increasing complexity of needs.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Real-terms spending per capita remains 27.1% below historic peak despite cash-terms CSP growth
findings.detail: While the council's Core Spending Power increases in cash terms, when adjusted for inflation and population growth, real-terms CSP per capita is projected at £1,478 by 2028-29, which is still 27.1% below historic peaks. Tower Hamlets has experienced the fastest population growth in England (22% between 2011-2021), meaning resources per head continue to decline despite apparent gains.
findings.matters: The council's financial capacity to meet resident needs and service obligations is declining in real per-capita terms, creating a structural sustainability issue that no transformation programme can fully resolve.
findings.figures: Real terms CSP per capita 2025-26 £1,226; 2028-29 £1,478; population growth 2011-2021 22% (56,200 additional residents); cumulative change in real-terms CSP per capita -27.1%
findings.quote: Real‑terms CSP per capita is projected to increase to £1,478 by 2028-29, but this remains below historic highs... Real‑terms CSP per capita remains materially below earlier peaks because population growth has outpaced the recovery in resources.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Worst-case scenario model shows £22.09m budget pressure in 2026-27 against £10m contingency, rising to £41.49m by 2028-29
findings.detail: The council's scenario modelling includes a 'worst-case' projection showing total budget pressures of £22.09m in 2026-27, £30.85m in 2027-28, and £41.49m in 2028-29 across demand-led areas (homelessness, adult social care, children's services). The council has allocated only £10m contingency in 2026-27, meaning it would be reliant on the £20m Risk Reserve contribution to manage the worst case—leaving no buffer thereafter.
findings.matters: The council's sensitivity analysis shows material downside risk that is only partially covered by its contingency and reserve provisions. By year 2-3, even mid-range adverse scenarios could exhaust available reserves.
findings.figures: Worst Case 2026-27 £22.09m; 2027-28 £30.85m; 2028-29 £41.49m; contingency budget £10m in 2026-27, increasing to £20m by 2027-28; total contribution to Risk Reserve £50m over MTFS
findings.quote: If the worst-case scenario occurred for all these areas the budget pressure would be £22.09m in 2026-27. The Council has £10m of contingency budget and £20m contribution to the Risk Reserve that could be used to offset the impact in that year.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Core Spending Power growth is 73% dependent on council tax rises, but Tower Hamlets' taxbase growth is slowing and it has the lowest Band D rate in London
findings.detail: Core Spending Power growth of £11.1bn nationally over the settlement period includes £8.3bn (73%) from council tax. Tower Hamlets' taxbase growth has slowed from a historic 3.3% to around 1%, and the council has one of the lowest Band D rates across the 33 London boroughs. The government's CSP calculations assume higher council tax growth than Tower Hamlets can deliver, creating a structural funding gap.
findings.matters: The council's resources are increasingly dependent on a revenue source it cannot fully control and where it is structurally disadvantaged (low existing rate, slow growth, high deprivation).
findings.figures: CSP increase £11.1bn nationally over settlement period; council tax share £8.3bn (73%); Tower Hamlets taxbase growth historically 3.3%, now ~1%; 1% council tax increase generates ~£1.5m per annum
findings.quote: After adjusting for the approximately £54m gap between the Government's council tax assumptions and the Council's own projections (reflecting Tower Hamlets' position as having one of the lowest Band D rates in London), the net improvement in deliverable resources is estimated at c.£91.7m.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Business Rates reset removes all accumulated local growth and resets baseline, creating forward funding volatility
findings.detail: The 2026-27 settlement includes a full reset of the Business Rates Retention Scheme that removes approximately £2.38bn nationally in retained growth, returning it to central control. Tower Hamlets' retained business rates are estimated at £180m in 2026-27 but the reset, combined with revaluation and new multipliers, creates material downside risk for forward years. The new safety-net protection steps down from 100% to 97% in 2027-28 and then to 92.5%, increasing exposure to shocks.
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile and the reset removes the council's accumulated buffer. The stepped reduction in protection means the council's exposure to volatility increases precisely when protection is most needed.
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates 2026-27 £180.090m; £2.38bn reset nationally; safety-net protection 100% in 2026-27, 97% in 2027-28, 92.5% thereafter; 3.75% allowance for appeals assumed
findings.quote: A full reset of the Business Rates Retention Scheme removes all accumulated local growth, returning approximately £2.38bn nationally to central control for redistribution through Fair Funding 2.0.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: SEND deficit projected to reach £49.5m by 2028-29 with future years' funding unclear after 2028
findings.detail: Tower Hamlets' DSG deficit stood at £20.1m at the start of the year and is expected to rise by a further £9.4m in the current year. On current trajectories it will reach approximately £49.5m by 2028-29. Government will pay 90% of the deficit accrued to end of 2025-26 in autumn 2026, but the 10% (£3m for Tower Hamlets) must be funded locally, and the mechanism for funding 2026-27 and 2027-28 deficits (forecast at additional £20m) remains unclear.
findings.matters: SEND deficits are a material, growing liability that the council cannot easily control. The statutory override ends in 2028, exposing the council to a deficit it may have to absorb into the general fund without confirmed government funding.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £20.1m opening; Q2 forecast increase £9.4m; projected cumulative deficit £49.5m by 2028-29; 4,600 children and young people with EHCP aged 0-25; government grant covering 90% of deficit to end of 2025-26; 10% (£3m) non-grant funded
findings.quote: It is currently unclear how the 10% (£3m for Tower Hamlets) non-grant funded amount will need to be funded and how 2026-27 and 2027-28 deficits will be funded (forecasted to be an additional £20m).

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Budget Report 2026-29 and MTFS 2026-29 - Final
findings.headline: Homelessness funding gap: £28.1m in estimated pressures against only £15m growth allocation, with transformation savings assumed to bridge the gap
findings.detail: The council estimates recurring pressures from homelessness and housing options at £28.1m based on Q2 2025-26 forecasts, but has only allocated £15m of growth funding. It is relying on a transformation programme to deliver a minimum £15m cost reduction to balance this. If transformation delivers only partially, there is an unfunded gap.
findings.matters: This is the council's largest unmatched budget pressure, and homelessness is the most volatile demand-driven cost in local government. A lender needs to know whether this gap is real or assumed away.
findings.figures: Estimated recurring pressures £28.1m; growth provided £15.0m; transformation efficiency plan £15.0m; 3,200 households currently in temporary accommodation
findings.quote: Currently the Housing Benefit subsidy has been frozen at 90% of January 2011 Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates – even though temporary accommodation has become significantly more expensive over the past 14 years.

findings.paper_title: Executive Response to OSC Budget Report
findings.headline: £200k estate police patrols saving has been removed from the MTFS
findings.detail: A recommended saving of £200k from reducing estate police patrols has been removed from the MTFS—indicating either the saving could not be delivered or the council chose to reverse it.
findings.matters: Removal of planned savings from the budget plan weakens savings delivery credibility and suggests targets are under pressure.
findings.quote: This is no longer in the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Executive Response to OSC Budget Report
findings.headline: Council budget structure relies on risk reserve and contingency to cover overspends
findings.detail: The executive states that 'any overspends that cannot be managed through in year mitigations or underspends will need to be funded from the risk reserve', and has increased revenue contingency to £10m.
findings.matters: Operating budgets that cannot self-correct through in-year management indicate structural imbalance; reserves intended for emergencies are being used for routine overspend absorption.
findings.figures: £10m revenue contingency; risk reserve amount not stated
findings.quote: Any overspends that cannot be managed through in year mitigations or underspends will need to be funded from the risk reserve.

findings.paper_title: Executive Response to OSC Budget Report
findings.headline: £37.5m committed to Adult Social Care and temporary accommodation, with reserves held for their overspends
findings.detail: The council has invested £22.5m in Adult Social Care and £15m in temporary accommodation. The risk reserve explicitly exists to cover overspends in these areas that cannot be managed through in-year mitigations.
findings.matters: Demand-led and inflation-sensitive services; their prominence in reserve trigger planning indicates structural pressure on these budgets.
findings.figures: £22.5m Adult Social Care; £15m temporary accommodation
findings.quote: In addition to the risk reserve the Council has increased its revenue contingency to £10m and invested in services, for example £22.5m in Adult Social Care and £15m in temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Executive Response to OSC Budget Report
findings.headline: Council Tax collection and base growth assumptions revised downward to 'more prudent' levels
findings.detail: The council has revised its MTFS assumptions for Council Tax collection and base growth to reflect 'more prudent assumptions based on recent data trends'. It is implementing a targeted collection programme with early resident engagement, new recovery procedures, and weekly performance oversight to strengthen collection rates.
findings.matters: Downward revision of Council Tax collection assumptions signals anticipated revenue shortfall; Council Tax is a primary revenue source and a leading indicator of financial stress.
findings.figures: No specific shortfall quantified; £10m revenue contingency increase mentioned alongside this
findings.quote: The assumptions for Council Tax collection and base growth have been revised as part of the MTFS and reflect more prudent assumptions based on recent data trends.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement Report - Council
findings.headline: Council's investment portfolio is declining
findings.detail: Section 3.13 explicitly notes that the Council's held investment funds are "Although reducing", with surplus cash concentrated in short-term unsecured bank deposits and money market funds, indicating a more cautious liquidity position.
findings.matters: Declining liquid reserves affect financial flexibility and the council's capacity to handle unexpected costs or borrowing costs without tapping debt markets.
findings.figures: "significant invested funds" (amount not disclosed in this excerpt)
findings.quote: Although reducing, the Council holds significant invested funds, representing income received in advance of expenditure plus balances and reserves held.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement Report - Council
findings.headline: Council will not budget for voluntary repayment of HRA debt
findings.detail: Section 3.12 states there will be no voluntary revenue provision (VRP) for HRA debt; instead, resources are being directed to housing investment and new build programmes. Only mandatory debt repayment will occur.
findings.matters: HRA debt repayment pace affects long-term HRA financial sustainability and creates dependency on the mandatory repayment schedule.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: To maximise resources available for investment in the existing stock and the new build programme, there will be no budgeted VRP to repay HRA debt.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement Report - Council
findings.headline: HRA interest cover ratio capped at 1.15, constraining housing borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Section 3.12 sets a maximum interest cover ratio of 1.15 for HRA debt. This is explicitly stated as a change that has been discussed with advisors and aligns with other London boroughs. Interest cover constrains how much additional housing revenue borrowing can be supported.
findings.matters: This hard ceiling directly limits the council's ability to borrow further for housing investment and new build, affecting housing strategy deliverability.
findings.quote: In order to assess borrowing affordability and constraints in the HRA, the Council will ensure that the interest cover ratio does not exceed 1.15.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement Report - Council
findings.headline: The s151 Officer role is held by an Acting director
findings.detail: The report is signed by Abdulrazak Kassim as Acting Corporate Director Resources, and Paul Audu as Interim Head of Pensions & Treasury. Neither title suggests a substantive, permanent appointment to these critical financial governance roles.
findings.matters: The s151 officer's stability and permanence directly affects financial governance credibility and lender confidence in the council's financial leadership.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Report of: Abdulrazak Kassim, Acting Corporate Director Resources

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - TMSS Mid-Year Report F
findings.headline: Council to require £53.7m new borrowing in 2025-26 to fund capital programme
findings.detail: Liability benchmark analysis forecasts the council must borrow £53.7m in 2025-26 and £76.9m in 2026-27 to fund capital spending plans. This doubles the council's current external borrowing of £68.7m over two years. At the prevailing PWLB 10-year certainty rates of 5.17%-5.62%, this will materially increase debt servicing costs in the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Large increases in external borrowing at elevated rates affect debt serviceability and revenue sustainability. With the capital financing requirement forecast to rise from £629.3m to £648.6m, the council is entering a period of significant capital-driven borrowing.
findings.figures: £53.7m borrowing 2025-26, £76.9m in 2026-27; current external borrowing £68.7m; CFR increasing from £629.271m to £648.637m; PWLB rates 5.17%-5.62%
findings.quote: the liability benchmark suggests the Council will require a minimum level of new borrowing of c£53.7m in 2025-26 and c£76.9m in 2026-27 to maintain the minimum investment level of c£60m at year-end.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - TMSS Mid-Year Report F
findings.headline: PFI and finance lease debt forecast to breach prudential limit at year-end 2025-26
findings.detail: The council's forecast PFI and finance lease debt of £74.5m at 31 March 2026 will exceed both its operational boundary of £61m and approach its authorised limit of £71m. This represents a governance breach of the council's own prudential code. The paper notes the position will be closely monitored with necessary adjustments actioned through appropriate governance procedures.
findings.matters: Breaches of prudential limits signal defective financial planning and debt control to lenders. The council is already above its operational boundary and forecast to exceed it further, raising questions about expenditure management discipline.
findings.figures: £74.5m forecast (31.3.26) vs £61.0m operational boundary and £71.0m authorised limit; actual at 31.3.25 was £72.716m
findings.quote: As at the time of preparing this mid-year report, the forecast PFI and Finance leases debt for 2025/26 is £74.5m at year-end. This would exceed the Council's operational boundary and authorised limits for PFI and Finance leases for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D-H - Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Authorized external debt limit rises 29% to £912m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council progressively increases its authorized limit for total external debt from £709m in 2025/26 to £732m, £784m, and £912m in 2028/29. This sustained growth in authorized headroom reflects anticipated borrowing expansion.
findings.matters: Authorized limits are set based on forecasted borrowing need. Year-on-year increases of £23-£128m signal the council expects substantial growth in total debt obligations relative to current levels.
findings.quote: Authorised limit – total external debt 709.000 732.000 784.000 912.000

findings.paper_title: Appendix D-H - Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Total capital expenditure plan nearly triples from £118m to £320m over three years
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure grows from £118.021m in 2024/25 to £244.595m in 2025/26 and reaches £319.606m in 2026/27. The HRA accounts for 65% of the 2026/27 budget, while general fund capital also increases materially.
findings.matters: Capital growth of this scale implies major program expansion, substantial new borrowing obligations, and potential changes to service delivery or asset strategy that alter the council's financial risk profile.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D-H - Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account borrowing forecast to escalate from £11.3m in 2026/27 to £108.1m by 2028/29
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account borrowing grows from £2.193m in 2024/25 through £11.324m in 2026/27, then accelerates sharply to £45.955m in 2027/28 and £108.131m in 2028/29. This represents a fundamental shift in the council's housing capital financing strategy.
findings.matters: For lenders, this signals a major expansion of HRA debt that will materially increase the council's debt portfolio and annual service costs. The speed and magnitude require understanding what drives this investment.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Anti-Fraud - Progress Report
findings.headline: Internal Audit plan delivery has slipped, with planned audit work being deferred or cancelled for 2025-26
findings.detail: Follow-up work on implementing prior audit recommendations has consumed significant audit team resources, causing slippage in delivery of the planned 2025-26 audit engagements. Planned audit work is being reprioritised, deferred to 2026-27, or cancelled entirely.
findings.matters: The inability to deliver the planned audit program suggests either resource constraints or that the volume of prior control failures requiring follow-up is exceeding the team's capacity, both indicating governance stress and unassessed audit risk.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: During this period much of the focus of the team has remained on the follow up exercise and this has resulted in some slippage in delivery of the planned audit engagements for 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Anti-Fraud - Progress Report
findings.headline: Four audits received Limited or No Assurance opinions, including payroll compliance, staff recruitment, and fleet management
findings.detail: Beyond PCN income, three additional audits received Limited or No Assurance opinions: Staff Recruitment and Pre-recruitment checks, IR35 and Off Payroll Engagement, and Transport Fleet Management. This pattern across HR, compliance, and operations suggests systemic control weaknesses across multiple functions.
findings.matters: Multiple control failures across different operational areas suggest governance issues that extend beyond a single function. IR35 and off-payroll weaknesses raise employment law and tax compliance risk; recruitment control weaknesses affect safeguarding; fleet management issues could indicate asset waste.
findings.figures: 4 audits with Limited or No Assurance: Staff Recruitment and Pre-recruitment checks, PCN Income Debt Recovery and Write-offs, Transport Fleet Management, IR35 and Off Payroll Engagement

findings.headline: PCN Income Debt Recovery and Write-offs audit received Limited Assurance, indicating control weakness in parking fine collection
findings.detail: Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) income debt recovery and write-offs received a Limited Assurance opinion. PCN income is a material revenue stream for local authorities. Limited Assurance indicates control weaknesses in debt collection procedures, write-off approval, and income accounting.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in PCN debt recovery and write-off procedures could result in revenue leakage, incomplete collection of due amounts, or improper accounting treatment, affecting both council cash flow and reported revenue.
findings.figures: Not quantified in report
